confidence_note: Book text not read. That Harari says scanners predict decisions before awareness is sourced to page-referenced notes; that he cites Libet is stated by commentators. Experiment numbers come from the 1983 paper as summarised by an outside source and are labelled in the story. Old text dropped: wrong timing (300-500 ms), electrode on the hand, the criminal-responsibility section.
facts: Chapter 8, The Time Bomb in the Laboratory: Harari calls free will a factual claim that conflicts with science. Brain processes are deterministic, random or a mix, and none of those is free. Acting on a desire is not choosing it.
Scanners can predict desires and decisions before people are aware of them, with signals appearing from a few hundred milliseconds to a few seconds ahead.
Commentators say the book cites Benjamin Libet's experiment for this.

Libet, 1983: a custom clock whose dot turned once every 2.56 seconds. Subjects flexed a wrist whenever they felt like it and reported the clock position when they first felt the urge. Scalp electrodes showed the readiness potential about 550 ms before the flex; the reported urge came about 200 ms before. Six subjects, forty trials each.
Libet himself proposed a "free won't": a veto in the last 150 ms before movement.
Later reanalysis (Schurger 2012) showed the readiness potential can arise from spontaneous noise. A 2021 review says the classic reading as a decision signal is no longer the field default.
Harari adds that drugs, genetic engineering or brain stimulation could create or erase feelings such as love or fear.
scene_details: A clock dot turning once every 2.56 seconds
A wrist flexed whenever the subject felt like it
Scalp electrodes recording before the urge was felt
tension: A signal appears in the brain about 350 ms before the person reports wanting to move.
opening_idea: Start with the clock dot and the wrist flex.

lessons.idea: A feeling of deciding does not tell you everything about where the decision began, so hold your explanations for your own choices a little loosely.
lessons.anchor: In Libet's task the brain signal came before the reported urge, yet Libet kept a veto for the last 150 ms.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: Someone who snaps at a coworker and insists they chose their words calmly, then reads the message back.

reflect_final: Which choice of yours would look different if you assumed the reasons you give for it were only part of the story?

use_cases.situation: After an argument you defend your choice of words.
use_cases.move: Say you chose in the moment and want to look at what led there, like the wrist that moved before the urge.

use_cases.situation: A friend says they simply decided to quit.
use_cases.move: Ask what happened in the days before they felt decided.

use_cases.situation: You feel an urge to send a message.
use_cases.move: Use the last moment before sending as your veto, as Libet's free won't.

pocket_idea: In Libet's clock test the brain signal came before the urge; use the last moment before acting as your veto.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In Libet's experiment a brain signal showed up roughly 350 milliseconds before people said they wanted to move.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Libet had people flex a wrist whenever they felt like it and note a clock; the brain signal began about 550 ms before the move, the felt urge about 200 ms; Harari uses this against free will; later work questions the reading.
